evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration’s byway description highlights open marshes, stone walls, conservation areas and pre-Revolutionary homes, with woodland trails leading to ponds, mills and dams.

evidence.claim: It recommends about three hours to take in some of the route’s places.
evidence.quote: Plan on spending about three hours so you can enjoy at least some things.

evidence.claim: Local families donated the land on which the Shaker community was founded in 1792 under Father Job Bishop.
evidence.quote: Through a donation of land from local community members, the Canterbury Village was founded in 1792, led by Father Job Bishop.

evidence.claim: Its members farmed and sold seeds, herbal medicines, textiles, pails and brooms.
evidence.quote: They made their living by farming, selling seeds, herbs and herbal medicines; and by manufacturing textiles, pails, brooms and other products.

evidence.claim: They also patented a washing machine that won a gold medal at the 1876 Centennial Exposition.
evidence.quote: The Canterbury Shakers patented a washing machine, an accomplishment that was recognized by mainstream society in the form of a gold medal at the Centennial Exposition in 1876.

evidence.claim: A nonprofit formed in 1969 to preserve their heritage; Sister Ethel Hudson, Canterbury’s last resident Shaker, died in 1992.
evidence.quote: The last resident, Sister Ethel Hudson, died in 1992, and the site is now a museum, founded in 1969, to preserve the heritage of the utopian sect.

evidence.claim: Start in Canterbury’s village center, a separate community from the Shaker settlement, with its town hall, church, store and gazebo.
evidence.quote: Canterbury s village center, while not part of the Shaker community, is simplistically striking. The center is comprised of a 1736 Town Hall, Canterbury United Community Church, country store, gazebo, and public library.

evidence.claim: Continue toward the Shaker Village in the eastern part of town.
evidence.quote: The Canterbury Shaker Village is in the eastern part of the town.

evidence.claim: There, original and reconstructed Shaker buildings form the museum, with nature trails leading to ponds, mills, dams and the Physician’s Botanical Garden.
evidence.quote: 27 original Shaker buildings, four reconstructed Shaker buildings and 694 acres (2.81 km2) of forests, fields, gardens and mill ponds under permanent conservation easement.

flags: No cached source supplies the road’s construction history or a formal state designation date. FHWA documents byway identity and features; the history paragraph concerns the community and preservation, not road engineering.
FHWA gives 12 miles; material maps 6.5 miles. Scope cannot be reconciled from cache, so mileage is omitted.
Original-building counts differ: 25 in FHWA and the town article, 27 in the village article. Count omitted; four reconstructed buildings distinguished from originals.

New maples moment is a short corridor feature, placed between the center and village, not a precise stop. No coordinates supplied because no dedicated Wikipedia COORDINATES line exists. Evidence is too thin for 90 words without repetition.
Current statement that the last of the Shakers died in 1992 is narrowed to Canterbury; the village source also discusses Sabbathday Lake Shakers.
No site-manager page is cached to verify current opening arrangements; none are promised.
Canterbury town moment is slightly below 90 words after removing a redundant incorporation sentence. The maple segment is also deliberately short; additional route engineering detail is absent.
